en: Thus have I heard: the Sappurisa Sutta (Discourse on the True Person), the one hundred and thirteenth in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma of the true person and the Dhamma of the untrue person.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person?
Here, bhikkhus, an untrue person has gone forth from a high-born family.
He reflects thus:”
‘I have gone forth from a high-born family, whereas these other bhikkhus have not gone forth from high-born families.
He, on account of that high-born lineage, exalts himself and disparages others.
This, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
‘High birth does not lead to the destruction of states of greed, nor to the destruction of states of hatred, nor to the destruction of states of delusion.
Even if one has gone forth from a high family;’
"And he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma; he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.
Thus, making practice itself his priority, he does not exalt himself or disparage others on account of that noble birth.
This, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person has gone forth from a great family...
[as before] ...he has gone forth from a family of great wealth...
[as before] ...he has gone forth from a family of magnificent wealth.
Thus he reflects:
"I have gone forth from a family of great wealth, whereas these other bhikkhus have not gone forth from families of great wealth.
On account of that great wealth, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘Great wealth does not lead to the complete destruction of lustful states, nor to the complete destruction of hateful states, nor to the complete destruction of deluded states.’
‘He has gone forth from a family of great wealth;
yet he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma; therefore he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.
But making practice itself his priority, he does not exalt himself because of that great wealth, nor does he disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person is well-known and famous.
He reflects thus:
‘I am well-known and famous, whereas these other bhikkhus are unknown and of little influence.
By means of that renown he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a person of integrity, monks, reflects thus:
‘Indeed, states of greed are not brought to exhaustion by mere renown, nor are states of hatred or states of delusion brought to exhaustion by mere renown.
Even if one is not known and lacks fame;’
‘He is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, who practices with propriety, and who lives according to the Dhamma; he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.
Thus, making practice itself the internal standard, he does not exalt himself on account of that reputation, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person gains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
He reflects thus:
‘I am one who gains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, whereas these other bhikkhus do not gain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.’
Thus, by means of that gain, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, monks, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:

‘Indeed, gain does not lead to the exhaustion of states of greed, nor does it lead to the exhaustion of states of hatred, nor does it lead to the exhaustion of states of delusion. Even if one is not a recipient of robes,
almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, if one practices in accordance with the Dhamma,
practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma, such a person is worthy of honor and praise therein.’”
Thus, making that very practice his internal standard, he does not exalt himself because of that gain, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person is one who is learned.
Thus he reflects:
"I am one who has heard much, whereas these other bhikkhus have not heard much.
On account of that great learning, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘Great learning does not lead to the destruction of lustful states, nor to the destruction of hateful states, nor to the destruction of deluded states.’
‘One may not be learned, yet he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma; he is worthy of honor there, he is praiseworthy there.
Thus, setting practice itself as the priority, he does not on account of his great learning exalt himself nor disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma of a true person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person is one who is an expert in the Vinaya.
He reflects thus:
‘I am an expert in the Vinaya, but these other bhikkhus are not experts in the Vinaya.
He exalts himself on account of that expertise in the Vinaya and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
‘It is not by being a master of the Vinaya that states of greed, states of hatred, or states of delusion come to exhaustion.
Even if one is not a master of the Vinaya;’
"And he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, who practices with proper conduct, and who lives according to the Dhamma; he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.
But having set aside mere practice, he does not exalt himself on account of being a bearer of the Vinaya, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person is a preacher of the Dhamma.
He reflects thus:
‘I am a preacher of the Dhamma, but these other bhikkhus are not preachers of the Dhamma.’
Thus, by virtue of being a preacher of the Dhamma, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, monks, is the quality of an inferior person.
But a superior person, monks, reflects thus:
‘Indeed, by being a preacher of the Dhamma, states of greed do not come to exhaustion, nor do states of hatred or states of delusion come to exhaustion.
Even if one is not a preacher of the Dhamma,
if he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, who practices with propriety, and who lives according to the Dhamma, he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.’”
Thus, having made that very practice his internal standard, he does not exalt himself on account of being a Dhamma-preacher, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person is a forest-dweller.
Thus he reflects:
"I am a forest-dweller, whereas these other monks are not forest-dwellers.
On account of that forest-dwelling, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘It is not by forest-dwelling that states of greed, hatred, or delusion come to exhaustion; nor do they come to exhaustion through forest-dwelling.’
‘One who does not gather stores is a forest-dweller;
and if he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma, he is worthy of honor there, he is praiseworthy there.
Thus, setting aside mere practice as a distinction, he does not exalt himself because of that forest-dwelling, nor does he disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person is a wearer of rag-robes.
He reflects thus:
‘I am a wearer of rag-robes, but these other bhikkhus are not wearers of rag-robes.
He exalts himself on account of that state of being a wearer of rag-robes and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
‘It is not by being a wearer of rag-robes that states of greed, states of hatred, or states of delusion come to destruction.
Even if one is not a wearer of rag-robes;’
‘He is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, who practices with proper conduct, and who lives according to the Dhamma; he is worthy of honor there, he is worthy of praise there.
Yet, having made that very practice his internal standard, he does not exalt himself on account of being a wearer of rag-robes, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person is an alms-collector.
He reflects thus:
‘I am an alms-collector, but these other bhikkhus are not alms-collectors.’
Thus, by means of that practice of eating only almsfood, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, monks, is the way of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
‘Indeed, it is not by being an alms-food eater that states of greed come to exhaustion, nor do states of hatred or states of delusion come to exhaustion.

Even if one is not an alms-food eater, if he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives in accordance with the Dhamma, he is worthy of honor there and worthy of praise there.’”
Thus, making that very practice his internal standard, he does not exalt himself because of that practice of eating only almsfood, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person is one who dwells at the foot of a tree.
Thus he reflects:
"I am a tree-root dweller, whereas these other bhikkhus are not tree-root dwellers.
On account of that practice of dwelling at the root of a tree, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘It is not by dwelling at the foot of a tree that states of greed, hatred, or delusion come to destruction.’
‘One who dwells at the foot of a tree does not take up a roof;
yet if he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives according to the Dhamma, he is worthy of honor there, he is praiseworthy there.
Thus, setting aside mere practice as a secondary matter, he does not exalt himself because of that tree-dwelling, nor does he disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of a true person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person is a frequenter of charnel grounds...
he is an open-air dweller... [and so on].
He is a sitter …pe… he is one who accepts whatever seat is offered …pe… he is a one-meal eater.
Thus he reflects:
"I am a one-session eater, but these other bhikkhus are not one-session eaters.
On account of that practice of being a one-session eater, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘It is not by eating at a single sitting that states of greed, hatred, or delusion come to total destruction.’
‘One who eats only one meal a day is not easy to find;
yet if he practices in accordance with the Dhamma, practices with proper conduct, and lives in accordance with the Dhamma, he is worthy of honor there, he is praiseworthy there.
Thus, making practice itself his internal standard, he does not exalt himself because of that practice of eating only one meal a day, nor does he disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma of a true person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
He reflects thus:
‘I am one who has attained the first jhāna, but these other bhikkhus are not attainers of the first jhāna.
He thus exalts himself on account of that attainment of the first jhāna and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a person of integrity, monks, reflects thus:
"The Blessed One has said that even for the attainment of the first jhāna there is non-identification.
For whatever one conceives, it becomes otherwise than that."
Thus, making non-identification the very basis, he does not exalt himself on account of that attainment of the first jhāna, nor does he disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma of a true person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a true person enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration... [and so forth].
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna.
He reflects thus:
‘I am one who has attained the fourth jhāna, but these other bhikkhus have not attained the fourth jhāna.
He exalts himself on account of that attainment of the fourth jhāna and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
"The Blessed One has said that even in the attainment of the fourth jhāna there is non-identification.
For whatever they conceive, that becomes otherwise."
Thus, making non-identification the very basis, through that attainment of the fourth jhāna, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the dhamma of a true person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Thus he reflects:
"I am one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, whereas these other bhikkhus have not attained the sphere of infinite space.
He exalts himself on account of that attainment of the sphere of infinite space and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘The Blessed One has indeed spoken of non-identification even with the attainment of the base of infinite space.’”
‘For whatever one conceives, that becomes otherwise.
Having made non-identification with that very state his inner standard, he neither exalts himself because of that attainment of the base of infinite space, nor disparages others.
This too, monks, is the quality of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, "Consciousness is infinite.
He reflects thus:
"I am one who has attained the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, but these other monks are not attainers of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness."
Thus, by means of that attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, monks, is the character of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
“The Blessed One has also spoken of non-identification with the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness.
For whatever they conceive, that becomes otherwise.
Thus, making non-identification his very inner core, he does not, by means of that attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, exalt himself or disparage others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the character of a true person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, an untrue person, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
He reflects thus:
‘I am one who has attained the sphere of nothingness, but these other bhikkhus have not attained the sphere of nothingness.
He exalts himself on account of that attainment of the sphere of nothingness and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, monks, reflects thus:
"The Blessed One has said that even for the attainment of the base of nothingness there is non-identification.
For whatever one conceives, it becomes otherwise than that."
Thus, having made non-identification the very basis, he does not exalt himself on account of that attainment of the base of nothingness, nor does he disparage others.
This too, monks, is the Dhamma of a true person.
Furthermore, monks, an untrue person, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus he reflects:
“I am an attainer of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, whereas these other bhikkhus are not attainers of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
On account of that attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he exalts himself and disparages others.
This too, bhikkhus, is the quality of an untrue person.
But a true person, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
‘The Blessed One has spoken of non-identification even with the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’”
‘For whatever one conceives, that becomes otherwise.
Having made non-identification the very inner core, he does not, by means of that attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, exalt himself nor disparage others.
This too, monks, is the dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, monks, a true person, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This monk, monks, does not imagine anything, does not imagine anywhere, and does not imagine by means of anything.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The third discourse, "The Discourse on the True Person," is concluded.
